locator.heading: Dock

source_text:
MANY kinds of these are so well known, that I shall not trouble you
with a description of them: My book grows big too fast.

_Government and virtues._] All Docks are under Jupiter, of which the
Red Dock, which is commonly called Bloodwort, cleanses the blood, and
strengthens the liver; but the yellow Dock-root is best to be taken
when either the blood or liver is affected by choler. All of them
have a kind of cooling (but not all alike) drying quality, the sorrel
being most cold, and the Blood-worts most drying. Of the Burdock, I
have spoken already by itself. The seed of most of the other kinds,
whether the gardens or fields, do stay lasks and fluxes of all sorts,
the loathing of the stomach through choler, and is helpful for those
that spit blood. The roots boiled in vinegar help the itch, scabs, and
breaking out of the skin, if it be bathed therewith. The distilled
water of the herb and roots have the same virtue, and cleanses the skin
from freckles, morphews, and all other spots and discolourings therein.

All Docks being boiled with meat, make it boil the sooner: Besides
Blood-wort is exceeding strengthening to the liver, and procures good
blood, being as wholesome a pot herb as any growing in a garden; yet
such is the nicety of our times, forsooth, that women will not put it
into a pot, because it makes the pottage black; pride and ignorance (a
couple of monsters in the creation) preferring nicety before health.

    DODDER OF THYME, EPITHYMUM, AND

evidence.summary: No modern clinical or preclinical evidence was found for Rumex sanguineus regarding its traditional uses for skin conditions (itch, scabs) or internal fluxes. The absence of contemporary literature suggests these applications lack current scientific validation.

pubmed.title: Evaluation of antidiarrhoeal activity Rumex maritimus root.
pubmed.relevance_note: Supports traditional use for 'fluxes' via demonstrated antidiarrhoeal activity in root extracts.

pubmed.title: Evaluation of neuropharmacological effects of Rumex maritimus Linn. (Polygonaceae) root extracts.
pubmed.relevance_note: Investigates neuropharmacological effects, potentially relevant to 'choler' or nervous system regulation.

evidence.summary: Modern studies confirm antidiarrhoeal properties of R. maritimus root, validating the traditional use for treating fluxes. Neuropharmacological research also exists, though specific links to 'choler' or skin spots remain unconfirmed in current literature.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence supports Arctium lappa's traditional use for old ulcers and sores via demonstrated anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and wound-healing activities. While specific data on womb displacement or sinew shrinking is absent in current literature, the plant's broad anti-inflammatory profile offers a plausible mechanistic basis for managing phlegm-related inflammation.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence offers limited support: R. maritimus shows antidiarrhoeal activity (PMID:12648830), partially aligning with 'fluxes'. Other claims lack clinical validation or contradict safety profiles regarding oxalates.
concordance.uncertainty: High uncertainty due to absence of EMA approval and limited human trials for most historical indications.
